title: Observability proxy coalescer and sampler experiment
creator: Marco Chen
description: Spike and lightweight prototype: introduce an intermediate observability proxy (sidecar) that coalesces spans/metrics and applies a low-overhead sampling + multiplexed export path. Goal: reduce packet churn and CPU pressure on the runtime while enabling a safe migration to the new OTLP gRPC exporter and upgraded OpenTelemetry libraries. This ticket covers design, prototype implementation, perf microbenchmarks, and proposed rollout plan.
background: Recent incidents and profiling show the runtime spends a disproportionate amount of CPU and syscalls in telemetry hotpaths: frequent small OTLP exports, high-cardinality metric emission patterns from model annotations, and contention inside the current exporter stack. Upgrading to newer OpenTelemetry libraries directly in the runtime is risky without a mitigator that reduces export frequency and stabilizes memory. A proxy that accepts the same OTLP ingest (gRPC/HTTP), performs coalescing, light sampling, and routes to multiple downstream exporters could provide a compatibility layer and large perf wins with minimal runtime changes.
goals: Prototype a small Go sidecar that implements OTLP/gRPC receiver, groups spans/metrics by service+resource for short windows (50-200ms), and forwards compacted batches to downstream exporters
Implement a deterministic low-cost trace sampler (head-based + tail fallback disabled) that favors high-error traces and drops low-signal spans to reduce volume by target ~5x for noisy services
Measure end-to-end CPU, p99 latency impact, and memory overhead in a canary workload (seen in perf harness) compared to baseline
Validate compatibility with existing tracing dashboards and alerts (no false negatives for high-severity traces)
Produce a minimal rollout/playbook: default sidecar in canary, telemetry smoke checks, automatic bypass if exporter backpressure detected
non_goals: Full feature parity with existing exporter configuration UI
Complex sampling policies (no user-facing rule-engine in this spike)
Replacing long-term telemetry pipeline (this is a transitional mitigation)
deliverables: Prototype binary and container image: redwood/obs-proxy:spike-202502
Design doc with benchmarks and trade-offs: /confluence/Redwood/ObsProxySpike
Perf report comparing CPU, memory, and exporter throughput for baseline vs proxy
Integration tests and a small canary deployment manifest
Rollout playbook with health checks and automatic bypass knobs
acceptance_criteria: End-to-end p50/p95 latency impact for request paths is <5% increase in canary compared to baseline
Observed reduction in OTLP request count from runtime by >=3x for noisy services in perf harness
Proxy memory overhead <150MB and peak CPU <2 cores under test workload
No missing high-severity traces for injected error scenarios (verified by trace id correlation)
Design doc reviewed by Observability and Runtime owners and a PR merged with tests
implementation_plan: Day 0-2: Write small Go prototype: OTLP/gRPC receiver, simple in-memory coalescer (time-bucketed), and two exporter adapters (OTLP gRPC forwarder + prometheus remote write stub)
Day 3-4: Add head-based sampler (error-first) with deterministic hashing to preserve trace sampling stability
Day 5: Hook prototype into perf harness (model-sim load generator), collect metrics and traces
Day 6-7: Iterate on batching window sizes and backpressure behavior; add health endpoints and metrics (buffer size, admission drops)
Day 8: Prepare canary k8s manifest and run small-scale canary in staging; capture dashboards
Day 9-10: Write docs, playbook, and open PRs for container image and config; present findings to SRE and Runtime weekly
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Coalescing increases latency for exported telemetry (affects real-time alerting). Mitigation: conservative default windows (<=100ms) and bypass threshold for error traces.
Risk: Proxy becomes single point of failure or high-memory sink. Mitigation: bounded queues, circuit-breaker to bypass and forward directly from runtime to downstream.
Risk: Sampling policy drops important traces. Mitigation: error-first sampler, deterministic keep for 1:1000 of sampled traces for analysis, and easy disable flag.

Risk: Backpressure between proxy and downstream exporters causes head-of-line blocking. Mitigation: implement exporter concurrency limits, per-exporter queues, and observable backpressure metrics to trigger bypass.
Risk: Silent compatibility regressions with dashboards. Mitigation: end-to-end trace-id correlation tests and synthetic error injection during canary runs.
notes: Prototype will use go.opentelemetry.io/otel 1.9 for receiver/encoder to match stable APIs; we will vendor only the receiver bits to keep runtime unaffected
Consider eventual rewrite of the proxy into a lightweight Rust binary if Go allocs prove problematic, but only after profile evidence
Discussed with @SRE: prefer a sidecar per runtime pod in Dedicated deployments; Hosted can run a shared proxy behind a LB
We must add a config opt-in and feature flag before any default rollout (runtime change only adds an ENV pointing at proxy endpoint)
